utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: -- but we have decided to go on and I hope everybody is agreeing on that so we don't miss any further time. I see that both the accused present here in The Hague are in their seats. And I would ask then the registrar to call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. The case is IT-04-84-PT, the Prosecutor versus Ramush Haradinaj and other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. And Mr. -- Mr. Balaj, could you hear the translation or there is difficulty?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED BALAJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can hear it at the moment. Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Brahimaj, can you hear the translation?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED BRAHIMAJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: Good. Well, then, we should hear the appearances for the Prosecution today.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: Thank you. And for Defence. First for the Defence of Mr. Haradinaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, Ben Emmerson, together with Mr. Rodney Dixon and Mr. Michael O'Reilly, appearing today for Mr. Ramush Haradinaj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: Thank you. And for Mr. Balaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Good morning. Gregor Guy-Smith appearing for Mr. Idriz Balaj. Present also by my side is Djenti Zuberi [phoen]. He is the translator for both Mr. Balaj and Mr. Brahimaj in case there's any matters that need to be attended to during these proceedings immediately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: Oh, thank you. And for Mr. Brahimaj?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Richard Harvey for Mr. Brahimaj. Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: Good morning. Well, we are all aware that this is a Status Conference in accordance with Rule 65 bis of the Tribunal's Rules. And we are all aware also the aim of such a Status Conference. I have been informed about the Rule 65 ter Conference which took place yesterday and the Senior Legal Officer who present in guiding this meeting has informed me about what was happening and what we are going to discuss further today. I would say orally now that after having heard about the discussions -- the issues which were up for discussion yesterday, I have decided that we are going to have a 65 ter meeting again in about --by the end of March, in about six weeks' time. And we have thought of - but that will be discussed further with the parties - we have thought of the 30th March, and I have decided that I, myself, will participate during that meeting so that we can all work together in time to see this trial prepared timely, as planned. So I ask the parties to have this mind during this conference today so that you are aware that already in a rather short time we will have a more thorough discussion on all the points which has been discussed yesterday. The Senior Legal Officer announced to me that we can expect an amended indictment from the Prosecution. It was mentioned to me that the Prosecution foresee that such an amended indictment would be presented by the end of April. I hope that the Prosecution would properly be able later to make it, at least in a draft stage, available for the next 65 ter meeting so that we all could be informed, also I could be informed, what we are -- what the Trial Chamber or I am expected to look upon according to Rule 50, when we are going to look on whether or not such a change could be allowed. I don't know if any of the parties have any further remarks on this subject on the amendment of the indictment or we could just take note of what has been said already. Have the Prosecution any remarks on this issue, or should we wait for the 65 ter meeting? It's up to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: Well, I think it would be useful for me to be informed now. Thank you. So if you will continue now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour. The OTP intends to bring four main amendments to the indictment, one only will bring in the new charges. I think the Defence still hasn't heard the interpretation of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me, I hate to interrupt. We seem to be having a moment of translation problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: Okay. Let's try a solve it. It has been solved or? Could anybody indicate, is it all right now?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, it seems to be all right when we speak in English. I'm not sure if it's all right when we're speaking in French.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: This is a test from the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: All systems are go again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: Okay. Fine. Thank you. Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Three types of amendments. One should lead to the creation of new counts, strictly speaking. It's very simple. In several counts, I exclude for the moment 21 and 22 counts, in these different counts there is an indication that a victim has not -- never been seen again. When there is identification -- forensic identification, OTP intends to -- I think there still is a problem --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now it's solved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: It's solved?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yeah, it's solved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: Okay. Okay. Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I suppose, Your Honour --I perhaps I should start from the beginning so the accused may have all the explanations or do you wish me to continue? When there is forensic identification, the OTP intends to update these counts, change the sentence, giving the name of the person identified. As you will see, this is not a new count; it's just -- specifies matters and contributes to give an -- up-to-date information. The second type of amendment which is envisaged, as you know, in 21 and 22 counts it is said that 22 people were killed and that forensic exams are ongoing to identify them there again, if we can identify them in a forensic way. The name of these people will be given. It is not impossible that we might create different counts for the identifications, but this will be formalised and there will not be new counts. We'll simply have -- we'll say that the body of the person was already counted, but in place of a violation of laws and customs of war, there will be no addition on the formal plain. The third type of amendment, and this is more substantive, essentially to add three new counts about incidents which have not yet been contemplated by the indictment and which have to do, respectively, with the three accused of different degrees of their taking part and to the joint criminal enterprise so that they all are concerned by these additions. In the counts which already exist, it might be possible that we might insert a few more qualifications or specifications, marginally speaking. But those are the main lines of what we intend to do, and we will endeavour to present you a draft when we will have the next conference, 65 ter, end of March. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: That -- yes, any remarks?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I should say I have a number of points I wish to raise formally and on the record of which this forms a part. And you have I think before you a schedule of dates which I shall turn to in a short time when the moment arrives. On that schedule, as you will see, there is an undertake that by the 23rd of February the Prosecution will outline the necessary particulars of the new counts to the Defence as well as the current proposals that it has for revision of any existing counts. Now, I should say that despite three meetings between Prosecution and Defence over the last few days since the beginning of February, it wasn't until yesterday that this announcement was communicated to the Defence, and as we understand it the Prosecution are still, as of today, not in a position to, or certainly have not, provided the Defence with any of those necessary particulars. And so we have insisted upon and agreed upon the date of the 23rd of February for communication to the Defence of the essential particulars.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: Thank you. And that covers all the Defence, right, I suppose? Good. We will return to this then by the end of the -- this conference. Then I understand also, probably we should take -- take it all together after the remarks by Mr. Emmerson. We have the question of redactions, and we have the question of witness statements which has not coming forward yet, I understand the -- in accordance with Rule 66(A)(ii). Yes, then of course there's also the statements or evidence in favour of the accused according to Rule 68. All of this, of course, need to be looked upon, but probably it -- it will be time for you --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: -- a more extensive intervention.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm grateful for that. And can I say that I propose to take it shortly because much of the detail was discussed with the Chambers Legal Officer at the meeting yesterday afternoon, but there are really five points that I need to place on the record for the purposes of the status hearing today. First of all, disclosure. Broadly speaking, the approach that has been taken thus far to disclosure involves, as we submit, a serious failure on the part of the -- of the Prosecutor to perform its disclosure obligations. Virtually every time that has been disclosed thus far has been the result of a specific request from the Defence. Very considerable efforts have been made by the Defence to obtain disclosure, but so far as the Prosecution's obligations are concerned, there has been very little tangible progress since this indictment was issued. That progress or, rather, the lack of it was reviewed yesterday afternoon, and I don't propose to go into details because it seems to me at this stage that is not productive. But as a result of the difficulties that have been experienced and perhaps, I don't know, due in part to the change of representation within the Office of the Prosecutor - we're now on our fourth Prosecutor - we finally, yesterday morning, managed to agree a series of deadlines by which the disclosure exercise would be conducted, because of course the dates which have been set out in the draft work-plan are nothing more than end dates. They don't, sadly, specify start dates and it is start dates that we now need for the Prosecution to perform their obligations. We, therefore, have drafted a document which you have before you printed on two sides of A4 which records accurately and in detail the deadlines that Mr. Dutertre agreed to submit to at yesterday morning's meeting. It has been exchanged between the parties and, indeed, amended at his request to reflect the present state of the agreed disclosure obligations. Indeed, the wording at the top, referring to those as undertakings, is Mr. Dutertre's insertion into the draft. Now, I do not understand the Office of the Prosecutor to have any disagreement with the substance of that document. It may be, because Mr. Dutertre indicated to this -- this to me this morning that he has some reservations about it being before the Chamber this morning. We do not have any such reservations. Indeed, we regard it now as axiomatic that the Chamber has close supervision over the obligations that the Prosecution must now perform, it having hitherto failed so seriously and so singularly to perform the obligations that it has. So that's the first point. I'll leave Mr. Dutertre to elaborate any concerns he has about the document, but as I understand it - and, as I say, we have had it passed between us with amendments made - there is nothing substantively in that version of the document which you have with which he disagrees. And obviously, it's entire for Your Honour to decide whether that should be made an order or a clear undertaking which can then be reviewed at an early Status Conference at the end of March. But we would respectfully agree that an early Status Conference at which the Prosecution can be held to its obligations on that occasion, rather than merely reminded of them, is now essential. Secondly, there is in existence on disclosure a much fuller draft discussion document setting out the general principles guiding disclosure that the two parties are contending for. That document is not agreed because there are differences between us on some general principal issues that are reflected in that document. But the parties will endeavour to finalise that general document and to provide a copy to the registry as soon as ever possible and certainly in advance of the next Status Conference. That then is the first general heading. The second general heading, and you've touched upon it already, relates to redactions. And again, and with regret, I find myself having to bring to the Chamber's attention another serious systematic failure. This time a serious systematic breach by the Prosecution of the Trial Chamber's witness protection order of the 20th of May of last year. May I just briefly remind Your Honour of the approach that was taken on behalf of Mr. Haradinaj to the Prosecution's witness protection application. We took a good-faith approach of not objecting to redactions and anonymity until the point arose in the course of the Defence investigation where those redactions were obstructing preparation for trial. That point has now arisen. And as a result of that, we reverted to the Prosecution last month to request the lifting of certain redactions on a sample selection of witness statements. When those redactions were lifted, it became quite apparent that the majority -- the vast majority of them were not even arguably within the terms of the Trial Chamber's order or in any way related to witness protection issues. Indeed some of the material that had been redacted by the Prosecution was on its face and plainly exculpatory material, which far from being redacted should have been being drawn specifically to the attention of the Defence. If I can give you a general indication, of the requests we've made for the Prosecution voluntarily to lift the redactions that it imposed because they are improper redactions, 70 per cent of those requests have now been acceded to, which is an indication of the scale of the over-redaction that has been taking place in this case. And indeed the OTP, the Office of the Prosecutor, have reviewed a sample of the statements from the next batch of requests that we have made and have confirmed that a similar systematic failure is present there also, with a similar ratio of 70 per cent over-redaction. And I make it clear, as I did yesterday, that that process has caused significant difficulties to the Defence because the material redacted is essential to the investigation. It is the names, for example, of individuals alleged to be perpetrators, not victims or witnesses, but perpetrators for whose acts the Prosecution wishes to place at my client's door, and yet they were prepared to redact the names of the principal perpetrators, and Your Honour will see immediately how difficult that is to make of the Defence. We are told that there are insufficient resources in the Office of the Prosecutor for those remaining statements to be reviewed quickly and for the redactions to be lifted. We have pressed for immediate lifting of all of the remaining unnecessary and unjustified redactions, but we have reluctantly been driven to impose the tightest timetable that the Prosecution considers itself able to meet and as you will see from the document that we have provided to you, we have requested and the Prosecution have undertaken to lift the remaining redactions on the first tranche of requests by the 23rd of February. That is -- you'll see that in the second box under the 23rd of February, but that they require till the 15th of March to lift the remaining redactions. Well, may it please be clearly understood the difficulties that that timetable inevitably places the Defence investigation in, but mate it also be clearly understood that the 30th of March Status Conference will provide the opportunity to hold the Prosecution properly to account in that regard also and that then and only then will it be possible for the Defence on behalf of Mr. Haradinaj, and I should imagine those acting for the co-accused as well, to ascertain what it is that the Prosecution even legitimately claims to be arguably necessary in terms of redactions and then to consider whether it is necessary to seek the Trial Chamber's assistance having redactions further focussed and lifted. So that then is the second, as we submit, serious systematic failure. The third difficulty I touched upon, very late notice of the proposed amendments to the indictment, notwithstanding meetings that have been going on since the beginning of February and the Prosecution still not in a position to provide the Defence today with the names of the victims, the dates of the alleged incidents, or the precise particulars of the counts and requiring until the 23rd of February for those particulars, even on the new counts to be provided And finally, the fourth broad heading that was touched upon by Mr. Dutertre, it appears that since 2002 a process of re-examination of forensic material lying at the heart of this case has been taking place. And it has been taking place, no doubt, because it was apparent to anybody who examined the state of the forensic evidence as it stood that it was blatantly contradictory and inadequate. As a result, since 2002, we understand, the remains of those referred to in the indictment have been exhumed and the process of re-examination and DNA comparison conducted with the offices of the International Commission for Missing Persons. This is a lengthy forensic re-examination, the existence of which was not communicated to the Defence at all at any time after the indictment was issued and not indeed until last Thursday, the 9th of February. Now, again, may I emphasise, we have in an attempt to comply with the timetable set down instructed, retained a team of forensic experts to begin examining the case the Prosecution went to indictment on. We're now told that that case is going to change and that, in effect, the forensic case will be superseded. We have no notice of that. Time and money has been wasted. Our forensic team cannot get on effectively with the job they have to do until they know the case they have to meet, which the Prosecution is still not in a position to disclose and has indicated that the earliest it can be in a position finally to disclose is the 31st of May, the end of May. In other words, from the end of May the Defence will know the case it has to meet, in forensic terms in full, and the Defence forensic team can conduct the investigations they ought to have been being able to conduct since March of 2005. What we have succeeded in doing in the timetable you have before you is ringing from the Prosecution an undertaking that by the 6th of March they will at least convey to the Defence the gist of the fresh identifications, and you'll see the way in which that is put. The short point is, and I'm sure it will be apparent to Your Honour, that the Prosecution conduct of this case has been regrettable and falls seriously short of what the Defence and the Tribunal are entitled to expect. May I mention one final point, which obviously has some interrelation with the first four. We have before us a draft work-plan dated the 16th of September, 2005, which again regrettably the Defence did not see in full until yesterday, and there is simply one aspect of it which I would like to draw attention, since it doesn't appear, to us at least, to entirely reflect the way in which the matter was left in September, and that is this: It has been a clear understanding that the trial is scheduled to begin in beginning of 2007 with a possibility that it might move forward to the very end of 2006. And as you will see, on the existing draft work-plan it appears as though a date of November 2006 has started to take root. I simply want to make the position clear because if the current state scheduling is that there is a possibility that the trial might be moved forward into 2006, towards the end of the year, then plainly the catalogue of inaction that you are having to review this morning, as well as the principal new developments of fresh counts and a wholly new fresh forensic investigation make it virtually impossible to imagine that the process of bringing the trial date forward can now be achieved. And I think it right that we place that position on record today. I well understand that it may be the next Status Conference is the time when that issue can be finally resolved, but let it be clear now that we are in very serious difficulty. I haven't brought the issue to the Chamber in these terms before, but the point has now been reached at which the Prosecution, in our submission, need to be held account to do the job that they are required to do. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, your last point, your last remark, given -- gives me reason to repeat that it certainly is my intention that this case should be ready if the Trial Chamber here is ready to start the case already during November this year. And of course that brings a burden on both parties to work -- actually to work loyal in order to make this workable at all. We all have not only an interest but also an obligation to try to -- really, to hurry-up in this Tribunal. We are under close observation, as everybody knows, and of course every trial must be fair and prepared as it ought to be, but nevertheless it is serious that we are not moving -- have been moving further than we have in this case. I'm not blaming anybody. I know there have been, as already mentioned, the shifts on the Prosecution side and of course that could always create some difficulties, but anyhow I -- the reason why we are moving the next 65 ter meeting forward is of course that we want to have a close watch now on the preparation of this case. I don't know if the remarks from the Defence side gives rise to any response from Prosecution. If so -- I take it, from what I heard here, that what has been said now is covering all Defence lawyers, but let me ask especially.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That is absolutely correct. It is, I believe, covering all of us. Of course, Mr. Harvey will speak for his client. I am concerned, have been concerned, and raise the same point that Mr. Emmerson just raised with regard to the practical ability for the Defence to be adequately and properly prepared, given the lateness of disclosure and the new case that we will have to meet, which was not contemplated at the time that the work-plan was first put forth. I appreciate, for a number of reasons, not the least of which I have been involved in another case here, the Tribunal's concern with the completion strategy, but I also am concerned, as I'm sure all of us are, that the completion strategy may well impact negatively on the right of the accused to have a fair trial, which is something that I believe a former Judge, Judge Hunt, at one point commented on and had some concerns about. Now, I am very concerned that a November trial date may, in effect, cause some serious inability for the Defence to be properly and adequately prepared in this most serious of cases, and I want to make it very clear that with regard to Mr. Balaj's Defence, we do not believe at this time, based on the disclosure we have received, and the anticipated disclosure that we will receive in the coming months that we will be in a position to properly go to trial before 2007.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: Well, I take note of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If I may just add to what Mr. Emmerson and Mr. Guy-Smith have said, with which of course I agree 100 per cent. I've just looked at my notes of the September 65 ter conference, 65 ter bis conference, and the note I see noted there - and I don't have the transcript in front of me - is the possibility of a November trial date was at least discussed. We are now six months later, almost to the day, from that conference and we are not one inch further forward. And that places the Defence under, in our submission, an unfair and impossible burden of preparation. We are still not ready to begin that process of preparation for which the Prosecution has now had several years. And that is the question that calls into question the whole concept of equality of arms and fairness of the accused, with which I know the Court and the Trial Chamber is especially concerned. The completion strategy is of course important, and we, on our side, have no wish or desire to delay that by -- by a day. But fairness to our client is paramount in a case, particularly of this nature where there is so much unsatisfactory information forthcoming from the OTP. So we obviously will, with the far more limited resources available to us on our side, pursue this case and our investigations as diligently as we possibly can. But I just wanted to underscore that six months after that September conference we are still labouring under a disadvantage which the Tribunal should not have to be concerned about and which of course places us in an impossible position. I cannot, very honestly, I cannot see November as being viable or reasonable. And I just have to put that on record today. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Harvey. But I'm sure you also are taking into account that your client is placed in pre-trial detention, and that of course also is a reason why we all must try to finalise this case as rapidly as possible. I'm sure that's something you are fully aware of, but that's something which of course I also am aware of that we have this obligation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: I'm very grateful for Your Honour for drawing attention to that reality. I am hopeful that that may be resolved by the Appeals Chamber, and I'm hopeful that that resolution will come soon. But I know that my client wants his Defence run thoroughly and properly, and if it means that he has to sit an extra day in the Detention Unit, he will sit for as long as it takes, but that's another matter to be discussed in another place. But I thank you for the concern that you demonstrated in that regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: Thank you. Now the Prosecution. Your response to the concerns you have just heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Several comments or remarks which were detailed which have been voiced. In a preliminary way I would like to say how surprised I am in the difference of approach which I see today by part of the Defence counsel. We have had three meetings during the last three working days at the request of the Defence. We cooperated on both sides, and my impression is that today's conference gives an impression of another approach. I'm rather surprised, but I would say it is not essential, that several points have been discussed, the question of disclosure, the question of documents and work-plan, which I will include in my answer about communication, the question of redactions, amendments, and forensic elements. On the question of disclosure, first of all, this is what I will explain, I have heard about breaches, serious breaches, to the obligation of disclosure. As far as I know, OTP has started disclosing even this afternoon some exculpatory documents have been -- are being communicated, post mortem exams, and in general I think that it's because of the cut-off dates. I would like to know, really, if the OTP has violated its obligation. It has respected the work-plan which was decided in September of 2005. We have indeed held meetings to try and organise amicably things between the two parties, and these meetings -- four meets, one in December, three during the last three days, and several documents, different documents, which are -- were in the making have been disclosed or produced and they need to be finalised. I want to say that these documents are working documents which are communicated amicable by courtesy, and this is a global discussion which should lead to a global agreement and it is with this intention that the Defence should produce a document which for the OTP as an ongoing process and it -- the OTP is a bit surprised about its consent on this matter. We intend to continue discussions on the work-plan to try and proof it as fast as we can, and we are close to an agreement and it should be manageable and should be possible very soon that we can't consider that things presented separately has had the agreement of the OTP. The agreement of the OTP will be given on the whole a document when it's ready. This being said, we intend of course to produce and respect our commitments, disclosure commitments, in a continuous way and to go forward. Our position is that we are going to continue working on this, but one shouldn't say this is finalised in any way and what -- has the approval of the OTP in any way. We still have to consult, make a final agreement on this document. This leads me to speak also of the other document which was mentioned, a memorandum. I specified that the OTP -- this is only an annex to this document, the one you have now, and it is part of the whole. I would like now to pass to the question of redactions, redactions of documents, which is an important item. I have to recall that threats to persons, physical integrity of people, of victims and witnesses in Kosovo is a well-known problem. You have seen the report of Mr. Kajdar [phoen] last fall. Secondly, the OTP continues to have fears or concerns for certain victims and witnesses. Of course, thirdly in this context, the OTP has been very careful. That has never intentionally breached the order of the Chamber as far as protective measures are concerned for the witnesses, in favour of the witnesses. Therefore, when we have, I have to stress, very recently received the requests from the Defence to review a certain number of passages of the indictment, we answered in the following days. And this is what we intend to do for other requests which are to be forthcoming. So this is, again, evidence of our cooperation, cooperation on the side of the OTP, and I think this is a matter which can be solved definitely later. If the Defence is not satisfied, we can always use the remedies which are available if they consider there are problems of security for the victims which would justify a certain number of redactions. As far as the indictment is concerned, now, of course OTP will give details and we shall, as you invited us to do so, produce at the next Status Conference a draft which will contain all the necessary details for everybody's information before we have a finalised document. This will be disclosed and communicated at the date you yourself have indicated. And the OTP will recapitulate a number of points with a certain number of explanations. As far as the last point is concerned, the forensic documents which have been mentioned. It's a very long process, it is an ongoing process, and the results are, of course, rather -- we take some time to get the results, but I can already, as we discussed with the Defence, say that we have disclosed, obviously, regularly, what we received and it is not to say that it is only at the end of May cut-off date that all this information will be communicated. In the meantime, the OTP is disclosing information in order to have finalised this at the end of May. It won't be at the last minute. It won't take place at the last minute. I will conclude by saying that we shall respect this schedule for September 2005 -- which was agreed in September 2005. We will continue to have discussions with the Defence, and that perhaps the sort of alarming remarks made may be perhaps a bit premature. And the OTP will do its best to respect its timetable and its own obligations. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Dutertre. It's encouraging for me to hear that you foresee this cooperation between the parties, and you mention that disclosure is an ongoing process and you, as soon as it is possible, will make the process transparent for the other parties so that this really can go on in the most speedy way to ensure that we can have this trial starting -- starting as soon as the Trial Chamber will be ready. I suppose that the next 65 ter meeting we will have sufficient time and we, I'm sure -- I'll make sure that we have that to go into all details, also regarding what is really needed on Defence side, for instance, regarding this bringing their own expert on forensic experts -- forensic examination. I'm aware the way things are done in the common-law system; that's not what I'm used to. We have a more simple system, and let us discuss the necessity of having all those examination made once more. But I understand that that is what is prepared for and if it can be done in a timely way, then of course it can be done, but let us discuss it. So I think that we now could close this meeting, but before I do -- I do that, then let me ask if any of the parties have any other issues they want to bring up here. Yes, Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I simply return to the status of the timetable --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: -- that is set out under the heading "agreed list of undertakings on disclosure"?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Because although Mr. Dutertre did not indicate to Your Honour any disagreement with the record there of dates given yesterday, nor can he disagree with the use of the word "undertakings" because it is his word, not mine, he appeared to be suggesting in the short submission to Your Honour just a moment ago that the Prosecution does not regard themselves as being bound to keep to this schedule because he would like it to have been appended as an annex to a different document. Well, leaving the drafting history aside for a moment, it does, with respect, seem to me that one needs to emerge from today's hearing with clarity that this timetable must be met. And if that requires an order, then I'll reluctantly apply for one, but it may be that simply a clear indication from Your Honour that there being no substantive objections to that timetable, it having been the Prosecution's own agreed timetable, we can proceed on the basis that the Prosecution must meet that timetable and will be expected to explain themselves at the Status Conference if they fail to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Emmerson. That is my understanding as well. I wouldn't like to see it necessary to make any -- any order from the Trial Bench, from my side. I think I will take the word of Mr. Dutertre regarding the cooperation which is foreseen between the parties and that it is understood on both sides that the preparation is an ongoing process and that of course what needs to be disclosed also should be disclosed on an ongoing basis and not only on a final date. So I look upon this list of dates as have been given to me today as a working paper on which I will rely and I -- I suppose that also not only the Defence but also the Prosecution will rely since I understand that that is something which is the outcome of negotiations in good a faith between the parties. So let us leave the history of the preparation up till now aside, and let us go forward in the expectation that this is the working paper which both parties will work on and which we will return to on the next 65 ter meeting, where we will go in detail with all the issues. So I will ask if the accused have any other matter relating to their stay in custody, their health, or condition in detention to raise -- oh, yes, Mr. Dutertre. Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DUTERTRE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wouldn't like to continue the discussion on this point. Of course there will be cooperation between the parties, but since the document which was extracted from another document has been given, I want to give you the only global document which has to be finalised. I don't want to continue on this point. I just wanted to let you know. Here is the document in question.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, this document has not been agreed. When I left -- when I left the meeting, it was my understanding that we had a timetable document and nothing more than that we were dealing with for today's proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: Nevertheless -- nevertheless, I'm -- I have received this document and I don't know it now, but as I understand -- I have understood that this is not in any way an agreed document. It is part of -- on the Prosecution's side, they think I should have that for information as well when I have got this timetable as a working paper. So I -- well, have you any further remarks on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I have no further remarks on the document at this juncture; however, in the event there are further difficulties with the memorandum that has just been submitted to you by the Prosecution, which at this time is a creature of the Prosecution, there may need to be some discussion about the entire drafting history, which will raise a series of unpleasantries which hopefully we could all avoid.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Hopefully. I hope so. I do apologise for at this point of the hearing going -- appearing to descend into some sort of unseemly spat but I must just explain the position. This document that you now have was prepared by the Defence on the 1st of December as a result of the meeting - and all of the meetings have been at the request of the Defence, not the Prosecution - to press Mr. Waespi, who was the previous Prosecutor, for disclosure. It was served on the Prosecution on the 2nd with insertion for deadlines. It took the Prosecution two and a half months to insert those dates. And when the document was returned to us finally yesterday, it included a number of amendments, one you will see at paragraph 32 which sets out to rob the agreement of any binding force, because it specifically sets out the Prosecution's request that the content of the memorandum is not binding in any way. That's the reason why I have been asking that we have some clarity on the agreed timetable. This was not a schedule to the memorandum. I drafted both documents. This was a document that was prepared as a military -- yesterday's agreement. It is important that all parties know that we are proceeding on that timetable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: We are certainly. That's at least what I am. And I thank you, Mr. Emmerson. Now, do any of the accused have any remarks regarding their conditions in the Detention Unit?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I do not from Mr. Balaj --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We didn't hear anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, as far as Mr. Brahimaj is concerned, I have been in discussion with the Senior Legal Officer and have provided him with a written communication concerning my client's medical condition, which still unfortunately continues to give rise to concern. And I am grateful for his good auspices in offering to intercede and see that my client receives the client that he has long been denied.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: Yes, I have been informed about this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: As I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: And I know your letter has been sent to the deputy registrar. And I expect that we will get a written response so that we can inform you at least when we meet again.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: At least --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: At least at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: I would hope, if possible, before that time. May I raise just one scheduling issue with the Court. Since you have indicated, Your Honour, that you intend to attend the 65 ter meeting, is it also your intention to schedule a 65 bis Conference to follow that meeting? I'm just thinking in terms, we've got Thursday, the 30th of March is now set aside. Should we, in our calendars, also be expecting to be here on Friday, the 31st? I just -- it would help to plan my future a little bit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: I don't think, but I haven't decided on that. That is something we could discuss probably on the 65 ter meeting. But if we -- it all depends, I would say, but I don't expect that there will be a following Status Conference.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Thank you for that indication.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: Well, then we'll finalise for today, and we'll see each other again. The case is postponed.

procedural_notes.text: [The accused Balaj and Brahimaj enter court]
--- Whereupon the Status Conference adjourned at
